intro: A chain lock is a run of hardened steel links, normally wrapped in a soft fabric sleeve, that closes with a lock barrel to hold a bike to a fixed object.
Because the links articulate freely, a chain can be threaded around awkward frames, wheels and street furniture that a rigid shackle would never reach.
Each link is a closed loop of case-hardened or alloy steel, and the lock's resistance depends mainly on link thickness, steel quality and how well the barrel is built.
The fabric cover is more than decoration, since it stops the metal scratching paint and carbon, and it keeps rain and grit away from the surface of the links.
Locking is usually done with a key, although some designs use a combination mechanism, and the barrel or its cover is often shaped to shield the keyway from grit.
Weight is the trade-off for flexibility, because a chain of useful strength is noticeably heavier than a cable and can be heavier than a comparable U-shaped shackle.
suits: Riders who park at street racks, signposts or fences with odd shapes tend to value a chain, because it wraps around objects that a fixed shackle cannot encircle.
An e-bike owner who leaves a heavy machine outside for long periods may prefer a thicker chain, carried in a bag or looped around the frame.
Commuters who lock up at the same spot each day sometimes keep a heavy chain at the destination and ride without carrying its weight.
Lighter, shorter chains that can be worn across the body or around the waist suit short stops where the rider wants security without filling a bag.
Cargo and family bikes, scooters and other awkward vehicles are often easier to secure with a chain because the length lets the rider pass through frame and wheel together.
Anyone who regularly leaves a bike in a higher-risk area for hours at a time may choose a chain for its thickness over the convenience of a lighter lock.
check: Check the link thickness and the steel type the maker describes, and compare the figure with the value of the vehicle you intend to secure.
Measure the length against how you actually park, since a short chain may not pass through both the frame and a wheel before reaching the fixed anchor.
Find out whether the lock carries an independent security rating, and treat any rating as a comparison tool between locks rather than a promise about what a thief can do.
Weigh the chain before deciding, because a heavy model that stays at home is no use and a lighter one that gets carried every trip may suit better.
Look at how the lock is carried, whether that is a shoulder strap, waist wrap, frame mount or bag, and whether the cover will rub on your clothing.
Confirm how many keys are supplied and whether the maker offers a key-replacement or registration service, as losing the only key can leave the bike stuck.
care: Wipe the cover with a damp cloth when it collects mud or road film, and let the chain dry fully before packing it away so moisture does not sit inside the sleeve.
Put a small amount of suitable lubricant into the keyway now and then, working the key a few times, because grit and damp are the usual causes of a stiff barrel.
Keep the chain off the ground while locked where you can, and avoid dragging it across rough surfaces that might wear through the fabric and expose the steel.
Store spare keys and any code card somewhere separate from the bike, and replace a worn cover or a barrel that has begun to stick before it fails in use.

intro: A child seat is a purpose-made seat that attaches to a bike so a small child can ride seated behind or in front of the adult rider.
Rear-mounted seats are the common arrangement, fixed to a rack, the frame or a dedicated mounting plate, while front seats sit ahead of the rider on the frame.
Most designs combine a moulded shell, padded lining, a harness to hold the child in place and footrests with straps that position small feet away from the wheel.
Mounting systems differ, with some seats bolting to a frame bracket, some clamping to a seat tube and others sliding onto a rack that is designed to carry them.
Many seats recline slightly, and a few adjust for the child's height, so the same seat can stay in use as a child grows within its stated limits.
Because the bike carries extra weight high and to the rear or front, handling changes, which is why a child seat must be matched to a compatible bike.
suits: Parents who want to take a toddler on school runs, park trips or errands often use a child seat to keep the family riding together instead of driving.
A seat suits a child who is old enough to sit upright, hold their head up and wear a correctly fitting helmet, as set out by the maker and local rules.
An electric-assist bike can make carrying a child less tiring on hills, as long as the frame, rack and brakes are suitable for the added load.
Families who share one bike between adults may like a seat with a quick-release bracket, so it can be taken off when the bike is used alone.
Short, regular trips on quiet paths and low-traffic streets suit a child seat better than long rides at speed where the passenger may tire or get cold.
Anyone whose child is outside the weight and age limits for a seat, or whose bike cannot take one, may want to look at alternatives such as a trailer or a cargo bike.
check: Fitting and weight limits must follow the maker's instructions and local rules, so confirm the maximum child weight and any age guidance before choosing a seat.
Confirm that your bike is compatible, including frame material and shape, available mounting points, and any limit on rack or seat-post loads stated by the bike maker.
Ask how the seat is mounted, whether it uses a frame bracket or a rack adapter, and whether that system can be left on the bike or removed easily.
Inspect the harness, footrests, straps and padding, and check that the child can sit comfortably with the harness adjusted correctly and the feet held securely in place.
Read the local rules about carrying children on bikes, including any age rules and helmet requirements, which vary between states and should be confirmed with the relevant road authority.
Think about the rider's own comfort, including pedal clearance, heel strike on a rear seat, handling when loaded and whether the bike has a sturdy stand for loading.
care: Before each ride, check that the bracket bolts, harness buckles and straps are tight and undamaged, and that the seat has not shifted on its mounting.
Clean the shell and padding with mild soapy water and a soft cloth, and let everything dry in the shade so straps and foam are not damaged by heat.
Re-check the harness adjustment as the child grows or changes clothing, and replace any strap, buckle or foam that is frayed, cracked, faded or stiff.
Retire a seat that has been in a fall or a crash, and follow the maker's guidance on lifespan, because hidden damage can weaken plastic and fixings.

intro: A folding lock is built from several flat steel plates joined by rivets, which fold down into a compact bundle and open out into a rigid bar when in use.
When folded, the plates sit close together and are often carried in a holster that clips to the frame, a bottle-cage mount or a belt.
Unfolded, the lock reaches further than most U-shaped shackles, and its rigid plates give a different feel from a loose cable, which can be bent and coiled freely.
Each joint is a pivot point, so the quality of the rivets, the thickness of the plates and the tolerance of the joints matter as much as the lock body.
Plates are often coated or sleeved so that the folded lock does not scratch the frame, and some designs add a small cover over the keyhole.
The trade-off is weight, since a folding lock with a useful amount of steel is usually heavier than a light cable, even though it packs smaller than a rigid shackle.
suits: Commuters who ride to work and need something they can mount to the frame and forget until they lock up often settle on a folding design.
Riders who dislike a bulky U-shaped shackle poking into their back or knocking the frame often find the narrow folded profile more comfortable to carry.
People locking up at wide bike racks, fences or posts benefit from the extra reach, because the open lock can span a larger gap than a compact shackle.
An e-bike rider who carries the lock on the frame every day usually wants low rattle and a secure holster, so that the folded bundle stays quiet over rough surfaces.
Cyclists with several short stops in a day, such as cafe visits and errands, tend to like how quickly a folding lock unfolds and tucks away again.
A rider with a small frame or few mounting points may prefer a folding lock, since it packs into less space than a chain and can ride in a bag.
check: Look closely at how the maker describes the plates and rivets, because the joints are the part of a folding lock that differs most from other lock types.
Check the open length and the shape of the opened lock, then picture it around your frame, a wheel and the kind of rack or post you normally use.
Ask which mount or holster is included and whether it suits your frame tubes, since a poor mount can rattle, sag or even drop the lock mid-ride.
Compare any independent security rating as a guide only, remembering that ratings measure resistance to specific tools and do not mean a lock cannot be defeated.
Consider the weight you are willing to carry daily, because a folding lock sits on the frame all the time and added weight is felt on every ride.
Confirm the lock mechanism, key count and any replacement-key service, and check that the folded bundle does not touch brake cables or a battery housing on an e-bike.
care: Fold and unfold the lock gently, avoiding forced twists, because bending the plates sideways can strain the rivets and make the joints loose over time.
Rinse off road salt and mud with clean water, dry the joints thoroughly and apply a light lubricant to the pivots and keyway so they continue to move freely.
Check the holster clip and frame bracket every so often for cracks or play, since vibration from rough roads can loosen fixings and shift the lock.
Retire a lock whose plates are bent, whose rivets show wear or whose cover has split, and keep a spare key stored away from the bike.

intro: A bike helmet is a head covering with a shell and an energy-absorbing liner, worn with a retention strap so it stays positioned on the head while riding.
The outer shell is typically a thin moulded plastic skin, while the liner beneath it is usually foam designed to crush and spread an impact over a larger area.
Styles vary from vented road and commuter shapes to urban lids with extra rear coverage and fuller-face designs, and some include a peak, a visor or integrated lighting.
Some helmets add a rotational-impact system, a slip layer or a reinforced layer in the liner, intended to manage forces differently from a plain foam shell.
A retention system, usually a dial or ratchet at the rear plus an adjustable chin strap, lets the wearer tighten the helmet snugly to the head shape.
A helmet only manages impacts up to a limit, so it is not a substitute for careful riding, sensible speed and good route choices.
suits: Everyday commuters and recreational riders on paths and roads generally want a lightweight, well-ventilated helmet that is comfortable enough to wear for the full trip.
Riders of faster e-bikes may look for a helmet with extra rear and temple coverage, and should check the maker states it as suitable for that kind of riding.
Riders on rough trails, downhill tracks or technical paths often choose a helmet with a visor and deeper coverage, since low branches and sun glare are common there.
City riders who travel in low light may choose a helmet with built-in lighting, reflective details or bright colours, as a complement to proper bike lights.
Children and teens need a helmet sized for a smaller head, not an adult model adjusted to its limit, so size ranges should be read carefully.
Anyone riding on a mix of surfaces, from shared paths to roads, benefits from a helmet that suits the most demanding conditions they actually ride in.
check: A helmet must meet the standard required where it is used, so look for the standard marking on the helmet and confirm it applies to cycling where you ride.
Fit matters as much as features, so measure the head circumference the way the maker describes and try the helmet on, checking that it sits level and snug.
The helmet should not rock forward or backward, the chin strap should sit comfortably under the jaw, and the pads should feel even with no pressure points.
Compare ventilation, weight, visor, rear coverage and strap quality against how and where you ride, since a helmet that is uncomfortable tends to be left at home.
If the helmet has integrated lights, ask how it charges, how long it runs and whether it is meant to supplement, rather than replace, the lights required on the bike.
Note the manufacture date and the maker's guidance on replacement, and avoid a helmet that has been dropped hard, since unseen damage to the liner is possible.
care: Clean the shell and pads with mild soap and lukewarm water, avoiding solvents and strong cleaners that can weaken the plastic and the foam liner.
Store the helmet in a cool, dry spot away from direct sun and hot car interiors, because heat can degrade the materials over time.
Re-adjust the retention dial and straps whenever the fit feels loose, and inspect the shell, straps and buckle regularly for cracks, fraying or wear.
Replace a helmet after any significant impact and when the maker recommends, even if no damage is visible, and follow the maker's charging advice for built-in lights.

intro: A riding jacket is an outer layer cut for cycling or e-bike use, with a longer back, articulated sleeves and fabric chosen to handle wind, rain or abrasion.
High-visibility versions use fluorescent fabric in colours such as yellow or orange, which stand out in daylight, together with reflective panels that return light in the dark.
Reflective tape or piping placed around the torso, sleeves and back helps other road users pick out the shape of a moving rider when headlights fall on it.
Waterproof and windproof jackets rely on a coated or laminated fabric and sealed seams, with vents, pit zips or mesh linings to let warm air and moisture escape.
Motorcycle-style riding jackets add abrasion-resistant outer fabric and pockets for removable armour, a feature some e-bike and e-scooter riders look for on faster machines.
Details such as an adjustable hem, high collar, cuffs that seal around gloves and secure pockets let a jacket stay in place on the move.
suits: Commuters who ride at dawn, dusk or after dark often wear a high-visibility jacket so they are easier to notice alongside their bike lights.
Riders who go out in cold, wet or windy weather need a layer that blocks rain and wind while still letting sweat vapour escape during effort.
Delivery riders, shift workers and others who spend long hours on busy roads may choose a bright, reflective jacket for the extra visibility it adds in traffic.
E-bike and e-scooter riders who travel at higher speeds may prefer a more robust, abrasion-resistant jacket with armour pockets over a light packable shell.
Occasional riders who keep a jacket in a bag for sudden showers often value a shell that folds small and weighs little.
Group rides and organised events frequently call for bright clothing, so a hi-vis layer over everyday clothes is a simple way to stand out.
check: Lighting requirements vary by state, and a hi-vis jacket does not replace them, so riders should check their state road authority for what applies.
Check the fit over the layers you will really wear, and make sure the sleeves reach the gloves with your arms forward on the handlebars.
Read the waterproofing description, seam sealing and breathability, and remember that some coatings can wet out or feel clammy on long, active rides.
For hi-vis wear, check where the reflective material sits and whether it remains visible when the arms move, a bag is carried or a layer is added.
If the jacket includes armour pockets, ask which armour is supplied or sold separately and whether it carries a recognised standard marking appropriate to the intended use.
Consider ventilation, pocket layout, hood design and packed size, since a jacket that suits neither the weather nor the trip soon stops being worn.
care: Wash according to the care label, usually in cool water with a mild detergent, and avoid fabric softener, which can clog waterproof membranes and dull reflective material.
Dry the jacket away from direct heat, since high temperatures can damage tape, coatings and seams, and hang it loosely rather than leaving it damp in a bag.
Reflective and fluorescent fabric loses effect as it becomes dirty, scuffed or faded, so clean it regularly and replace the garment when the panels look worn.
Re-proof a waterproof shell with a suitable wash-in or spray treatment when water stops beading on the surface, and check zips and seams for damage.

intro: A bike light is a battery-powered lamp, usually LED, that mounts to the bike or rider so the user can see the path ahead and be seen by others.
Front lights are generally white and shaped to illuminate the ground or highlight the rider, while rear lights are red and intended to be noticed from behind.
Output is described in lumens, but beam pattern, optics and mounting angle shape how useful that light really is, so the figure alone does not tell the whole story.
Modes typically include steady, pulsing and flashing settings, and some add sensors that change brightness when the bike brakes or begins to move.
Power comes from a rechargeable battery charged by USB cable or from replaceable cells, and mounts range from rubber straps to clamps, seat-post brackets and helmet fittings.
Beyond lamps, visibility gear includes reflectors, reflective bands and clip-on markers that bounce light back toward a source rather than producing their own.
suits: Riders who travel before sunrise, after sunset or through tunnels and shaded paths need lights that let them see surface hazards as well as be seen.
City riders on well-lit streets often use compact lights that mainly make them noticeable, while riders on dark paths want a stronger beam that actually lights the road.
Daily e-bike and e-scooter commuters tend to prefer rechargeable lights with long run times, since swapping cells every few days becomes tiresome.
Riders who regularly lock a bike outside may want lights that detach quickly, so they can be carried with the rider instead of staying on the bike.
Group riders, children riding behind adults and anyone on a shared road can add clip-on markers or reflective bands as an extra layer of visibility.
Wet-weather and trail riders benefit from a light with a sealed body and a mount that stays put over bumps and spray.
check: Lighting requirements vary by state, so check your state road authority for what must be fitted and displayed when riding at night.
Compare the stated run times at each brightness setting rather than the headline figure, because the highest output usually drains the battery much faster.
Study the beam shape and whether it is cut to avoid dazzling oncoming riders and drivers, and check the angle can be adjusted once mounted.
Make sure the mount suits your handlebar, seat post or helmet diameter, and whether it can be moved between bikes or removed quickly without tools.
Ask about the charging method, the port cover and the weather resistance the maker describes, since moisture can reach the electronics through an unprotected charging port.
Think about a spare light or a second rear light, and check whether your state allows flashing modes or expects a steady beam.
care: Charge lights fully before long rides and recharge them promptly after use, since leaving a lithium cell flat for months can shorten its life.
Wipe the lens and body clean with a damp cloth, because dirt and road film dull the output and hide the reflective surfaces on markers.
Check the mount and strap before each ride, re-aim the beam if the light has slipped, and replace perished rubber bands that no longer grip.
Close the port cover firmly after charging, dry the light before storing it, and replace any unit with a cracked case or a battery that swells.

intro: A pannier is a bag that hangs from a rear or front rack, carried in a pair or singly, to move cargo from the rider's back to the bike.
Fixing hooks or a clip system at the top grip the rack rails, while a lower hook or strap stops the bag swinging or lifting off the rack.
Waterproof panniers use coated fabric with welded seams and a roll-top closure, which is folded several times and clipped shut to keep rain and spray out.
Other bags use a zipped main compartment, outer pockets and a lid, which are easier to open at a glance but depend more on a rain cover in heavy weather.
Capacity is measured in litres for each bag, and many panniers include reflective patches, a carry handle or a shoulder strap so they can double as a bag off the bike.
A single pannier, a dry bag strapped to a rack and a trunk bag are related ways to carry load, differing mainly in capacity, fixings and how easily they detach.
suits: Commuters carrying a laptop, lunch, work clothes and a lock find that panniers keep weight low and off the shoulders, which makes a long ride more comfortable.
Touring riders and those out for several days can load a full set, spreading the weight across the bike for a steadier ride than a backpack allows.
Shoppers and errand runners value a bag that clips on at the rack and off again in seconds, with a handle for carrying it into the shop.
Riders in rainy climates or on wet trails suit a roll-top, waterproof design, which helps protect clothes and electronics when a downpour arrives without warning.
E-bike riders with a sturdy rack and a motor to help with the load can carry heavier pannier loads, within the carrying limits set by the bike and rack maker.
Riders who want a lean sporty look often pick a small trunk bag or seat pack instead of a full-sized pannier.
check: Confirm that the rack is compatible with the bag's hook system, including the rail diameter and spacing, before ordering, since a poor match lets the bag rattle or slip.
Compare the stated capacity in litres with what you actually carry, and consider whether one bag or a pair is needed to keep the load balanced.
Establish whether the bag is waterproof or only water-resistant, and look at the seams, the closure and the fabric, which determine how well rain is kept out.
Allow for heel clearance, because a bag that sits too far forward can catch your feet when pedalling, particularly on a bike with a short rear end.
Consider the weight of the empty bag, the strength of the mounting plastic and metal parts, and how easy the fixings are to adjust with gloves on.
Look for reflective panels and a secure way to stop the bag bouncing off, and remember that stated rack load limits apply to the whole load, not each bag.
care: Rinse the bag with fresh water and a soft brush when it is muddy, avoiding harsh detergents that could damage waterproof coatings and welded seams.
Dry panniers fully, open and out of direct sun, before storing them, because trapped moisture can encourage mildew and unpleasant odours.
Inspect the hooks, straps and rack fixings occasionally for wear or loosening, and tighten or replace them if the bag starts to shift while riding.
Pack heavier items low and close to the rack, keep sharp edges away from the lining, and fold roll-top closures neatly so the seal stays effective.

intro: A phone mount is a bracket that holds a smartphone on the handlebar or stem so the screen can be glanced at for navigation, ride tracking or e-bike apps.
Clamp-style mounts wrap around the bar or stem with a screw or lever, while some attach through a stem cap or an extension that places the phone ahead of the bars.
The phone itself is held by a case with a locking interface, by adjustable spring-loaded arms, or by a clamp that grips the edges of whatever device is fitted.
Case-based systems twist or click the phone into place and are quick to remove, but they require the compatible case or adapter to stay on the phone.
Grip-style holders accept many phone sizes with one cradle, which suits shared use, though they can feel bulkier and may cover part of the screen edges.
Some mounts add a weather cover, a sunshade or a charging pad, but many are simply holders with no electronics.
suits: Delivery riders and couriers who check an app between stops value a phone mount that keeps the screen visible and the phone secure on rough surfaces.
Commuters following a map route can check the next turn at a glance instead of stopping to pull a phone out of a pocket.
Touring and leisure riders use a mount for navigation and ride recording, then take the phone off quickly when they reach a stop.
E-bike and e-scooter riders who monitor battery, assist level or speed through a companion app may want the phone in view on the bars.
Those who share a bike with a partner or family may prefer an adjustable grip that fits several phone sizes without swapping cases.
Riders who only use a phone for occasional navigation, or prefer a separate bike computer, may find a mount unnecessary and be happier with a small dedicated unit.
check: Make sure the mount fits your handlebar or stem diameter and shape, and that it does not collide with a light, a bell, a display or the brake levers.
Check that the phone model you own is supported, including its size, camera bump and any thick case, since not every holder suits every device.
Ask how the phone is released and held, and whether it stays in place over potholes and on corrugated surfaces, where vibration can loosen weak grips.
Vibration, especially from motorised bikes, may affect some phone camera systems, so ask whether the mount offers vibration damping and read the phone maker's guidance.
Weigh up weather and sun, such as whether a cover is available, how the screen looks in glare and whether the mount allows the phone to be angled.
Look up local road rules on phone use while riding, which vary by state, and set up navigation before leaving so the phone does not need handling on the move.
care: Tighten the clamp and any adapter screws evenly, using the tool the maker specifies, and recheck them after the first few rides as vibration can settle the parts.
Wipe the interface and the back of the case clean from time to time, because grit trapped between the surfaces can wear them and loosen the hold.
Do not over-tighten on carbon bars or thin-walled stems, and use any supplied shim or pad so the clamp does not crush or mark the surface.
Remove the phone when parked, keep rubber parts out of long sun exposure, and replace any holder with worn arms, cracked plastic or a weak lock.

intro: A rack is a metal frame fixed over the rear or front wheel to carry bags and cargo, while a basket is an open container fixed to the handlebar or a rack.
Racks are commonly made of aluminium or steel tube, with aluminium being lighter and steel often favoured for its strength and ease of repair.
Mounting is through eyelets on the frame and fork or through a seat-post or axle-clamp system for bikes that lack the threaded mounts.
A rear rack usually has a flat platform for a trunk bag or a strapped load, rails that hold panniers, and a mount for a rear light.
Front racks and handlebar baskets carry load ahead of the rider, which keeps it in sight but affects steering more than weight placed behind.
Baskets are made from wire, wicker, plastic or fabric, and some detach with a quick-release bracket so they can be carried like a shopping basket.
suits: Riders who regularly carry shopping, a work bag or a child's gear gain a stable, load-bearing platform from a rack instead of wearing a heavy backpack.
Commuters who like to throw a bag into something open and ride off tend to prefer a front basket for its easy access.
Touring and long-distance riders often fit a sturdy rear rack, and sometimes a front one, to take panniers and spread the load evenly across the bike.
E-bike riders who carry bulky loads often choose a stronger rack designed for the extra weight, within the load limits set for both the rack and the bike.
Casual riders after a relaxed look and a simple way to carry a picnic, groceries or a jacket often pick a wicker or wire basket.
Riders whose bikes lack rack mounts, or who use a full-suspension frame or a carbon seat post, may need a specific clamp-on design rather than a standard rack.
check: Check that your frame and fork have the eyelets the rack needs, and that the rack matches your wheel size, tyre width and disc brake or mudguard setup.
Read the stated load limit for the rack and, for a handlebar basket, for the bars as well, and compare it with the heaviest load you expect.
Ask whether the rack suits panniers, a trunk bag or another carrying system, because rail shape and platform size differ between designs.
Think about the effect on handling, since a loaded front basket changes steering feel and a loaded rear rack can raise the bike's centre of gravity.
Consider the material and finish, whether it is aluminium, steel or wicker, and how well it resists rust, along with the weight it adds to the bike.
Look for a rear light mount, a built-in reflector and a way to secure the load, such as elastic cords or a spring clip, for riding at night.
care: Re-tighten the mounting bolts after the first rides and then periodically, using thread-locking compound if the maker advises, because vibration can loosen a rack over time.
Wipe the metal clean after wet rides and touch up chips in the paint or powder coat early, so rust does not take hold.
Keep wicker or fabric baskets dry, brush off dirt with a soft brush and treat wicker with a suitable protective finish if the maker recommends.
Spread loads evenly, keep within the stated limits and stop using a rack that is cracked, bent or has a failed weld until it is replaced.

intro: A U-lock, also called a D-lock, is a rigid hardened-steel shackle shaped like the letter U that slots into a crossbar containing the locking mechanism.
The shackle is a solid bar or a hollow section, and a thicker bar generally takes more effort to cut or break than a thinner one of similar steel.
Closing the shackle into the crossbar engages a bolt at one or both ends, and a double-locking design holds the bar at both points rather than one.
The rigid shape leaves a limited internal gap, so the lock is most useful when it fits snugly around the frame and a solid fixed object.
Sizes range from compact mini models that pass around a frame and a rear wheel to longer shackles that reach a wider rack or a thicker post.
A rubber or vinyl coating normally covers the shackle and crossbar to protect paintwork, and some models include a bracket so the lock can ride on the frame.
suits: Riders who lock up in city centres, train stations or campus racks often reach for a U-lock, since a rigid shackle is quick to fit around a frame and a post.
Daily commuters like how quickly it clicks shut, which keeps short stops efficient, and the whole lock can be carried in a bag or on a frame mount.
Owners of heavier e-bikes who park outdoors often choose a larger, thicker shackle, accepting extra weight in return for a more robust bar.
A compact mini model suits someone with a small bike or scooter who locks only the frame to a solid post and wants a light, easy-to-carry lock.
People who prefer a simple, sturdy lock without moving joints or fabric sleeves tend to like the straightforward design of a solid shackle.
A U-lock is less suited to riders who regularly lock to wide or irregular objects, since the fixed shape limits how much it can wrap around.
check: Check the shackle diameter and the type of steel the maker states, remembering that a thicker bar usually means more weight as well as more resistance.
Measure the inside gap, then test it against your frame, the rear wheel and the posts or racks you use most before settling on a size.
Learn whether the crossbar locks at one end or both, as a double-locking design holds the shackle in two places and is sometimes preferred for that reason.
Read any independent security rating as a way to compare models, not as a promise, since a determined thief with the right tools can defeat any lock.
Consider how the lock will travel, including whether a frame bracket is included and whether it suits your frame tubing and keeps the lock from rattling.
Find out the number of keys supplied and whether the maker provides replacements, and look for a protected crossbar cover that keeps grit out of the keyhole.
care: Lubricate the keyway and the crossbar bolt openings with a suitable lock lubricant a couple of times a year, then work the key to spread it.
Wipe the shackle and coating clean after wet rides, and check the coating for splits that could let water reach the steel and encourage rust.
Avoid letting the lock fall onto hard ground, since repeated knocks can chip the coating and loosen the mount that holds it to the frame.
Keep spare keys separate from the bike, and stop using a lock that sticks, binds or has a visibly bent shackle until it has been replaced.
